subject: chemistry
question_text: Explain why diamond is an abrasive.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, IPE STUDY MATERIAL for Jr. Students — Chemistry (2026-27 edition), book p.107, chapter 9 p-BLOCK ELEMENTS GROUP 14, Short Answer Questions question 32(d). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints no per-step allocation on any answer in this chapter. The book prints no exam-appearance years for this question, so appearances[] is empty. SPELLING CORRECTED: the source prints 'Diamond dyes are used for drawing thin wires'. The word is 'dies' — a die is the tool a wire is drawn through — and this card writes 'diamond dies' and explains what a die is, because 'dyes' makes the sentence mean nothing. steps.label: The structure of diamond
lines: In diamond every carbon atom is sp³
hybridised and is joined to four other
carbon atoms by covalent bonds.
The bonds point to the corners of a
regular tetrahedron, the bond angle is
109°28′ and the C–C bond length is
The pattern repeats in all three
directions, so the whole crystal is one
rigid covalent network.
steps.why: An abrasive question is really a hardness question, and hardness has to be argued from the structure. The four fixed bond directions per carbon are what will make the crystal rigid two steps further on.
common_mistakes: Starting at the uses. Give the structure that makes diamond hard, and let the uses follow from it.
Answering sp² for diamond. Each carbon is bonded to four other carbon atoms, so it is sp³.
steps.memory_tip: Four bonds per carbon, tetrahedral, repeating in three dimensions.
steps.margin_note: Begin with the structure. Every later line in this answer depends on it.

steps.label: Why diamond is hard
lines: Each C–C bond in diamond takes
348 kJ mol⁻¹ to break.
There are no weak forces in diamond and
no layers that can slide, so an atom
cannot be pushed out of place without
covalent bonds being broken.
Diamond is therefore the hardest known
substance, and nothing but another
diamond can scratch it.
steps.why: Hardness means a surface cannot be scratched or dented. In diamond both would require covalent bonds to break, and every one of those bonds points in a fixed direction, so the surface stays as it was cut.
common_mistakes: Writing that diamond is hard because it is dense. Density is a separate property; the hardness comes from the rigid network of strong bonds.
Giving graphite's reason by mistake. Graphite is soft because its sheets slide, and diamond has no sheets to slide.
steps.memory_tip: Nothing weak and nothing sliding, so no atom can be pushed out of place.
steps.margin_note: State that diamond is harder than the material being worked; the next step needs that sentence.

steps.label: What an abrasive must be
lines: An abrasive is a substance used to
grind, cut or polish another material
by wearing it away.
To do that it must be harder than the
material worked against it, or it
would be worn away instead.
Diamond scratches every other known
substance, so it can grind, cut and
polish them all, and it wears away only
very slowly.
steps.why: This is the step that connects hardness to the word abrasive. Grinding is one surface scratching another, so the abrasive is simply whichever of the two is harder — and diamond is harder than every other material.
common_mistakes: Naming the uses without saying what an abrasive is. The definition is what makes the hardness relevant.
Writing that an abrasive must be heavy or rough. It must be harder than the material it is used on.
steps.memory_tip: An abrasive has to be the harder of the two surfaces.
steps.margin_note: Define the word abrasive in one line; it is what ties the hardness to the uses.

steps.label: Where it is used

lines.text: The hardest substance grinds all others

lines: Diamond dust is set into grinding
wheels, cutting discs and polishing
powders.
Diamond tipped bits are used for
drilling rock, and small diamonds are
used for cutting glass.
Diamond dies are used for drawing thin
wire. A die is a block with a hole in
it, and the metal is pulled through the
hole to make it thinner; a diamond die
keeps the hole at its exact size
because it does not wear away.
steps.why: The uses are the evidence that the hardness argument is right. Each of them is the same job — one surface wearing another away — and in every one of them diamond is the surface that is not worn away.
common_mistakes: Writing 'diamond dyes'. A die is the block with a hole through which a wire is drawn, so the word here is die.
Giving the gem use as an example of an abrasive. A gem is valued for its high refractive index, which is a different property.
steps.memory_tip: Grinding wheels, drill bits, glass cutters and wire-drawing dies — all of them cut or wear something else away.
steps.margin_note: One closing line naming a use completes the answer.

insider_note: A complete answer builds the argument in order: the rigid network, the hardness that follows from it, what an abrasive has to be, and then the grinding, drilling and wire-drawing uses.
